description: The origins, meaning and importance of Diwali and Holi for Hindus in Great Britain today.
content_html:
Hindu Festivals in British Life

Festivals are central to Hindu religious life. They mark time by sacred stories, bring communities together, renew devotion and express joy in the divine. Two of the most widely celebrated Hindu festivals in Britain are Diwali and Holi. Both are celebrated by millions of Hindus across the UK and both have meanings that reach deep into Hindu scripture and devotional life.

It is important to note that Diwali is also celebrated by Sikhs (as Bandi Chhor Divas, marking the release of Guru Hargobind from imprisonment) and by Jains. The festival’s meaning differs across traditions. In this lesson, the focus is on its meaning for Hindus specifically.

Diwali: Origins and Meaning

Diwali (also spelled Divali) is a five-day festival celebrated in late October or November, according to the Hindu lunar calendar. The word diwali comes from the Sanskrit dipavali, meaning “row of lights.” The festival is known as the Festival of Lights.

The most widely known origin story is from the Ramayana: after Rama’s victory over the demon Ravana and his 14-year exile, he and Sita returned to their kingdom of Ayodhya. The people of Ayodhya lit rows of clay lamps (diyas) to welcome them home and to light their way through the dark. This story celebrates the triumph of righteousness over evil and the return of the divine king.

In Vaishnavite communities, Diwali is also associated with the worship of Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and prosperity. On the main Diwali night, homes are lit with lamps and decorated with rangoli (intricate patterns made from coloured powder) to welcome Lakshmi in. Worshippers perform puja to Lakshmi and pray for prosperity and wellbeing in the coming year.

In South India, Diwali is associated with Krishna’s defeat of the demon Narakasura — showing that even within Hinduism, the same festival can have different origin stories in different regional traditions.

Key Fact

Diwali primary meanings: (1) Rama’s return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana — triumph of righteousness over evil; (2) worship of Lakshmi, goddess of wealth and prosperity. The lighting of diyas symbolises the triumph of light over darkness.

Diwali in Great Britain Today

The Hindu community in Britain celebrates Diwali with great enthusiasm. In Leicester, which has one of the largest Hindu populations outside India, the Diwali celebrations on Belgrave Road attract hundreds of thousands of visitors each year and include one of the largest Diwali parades outside Asia. The BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Neasden holds special puja and events throughout the festival period.

Meena, a 72-year-old grandmother who came from Gujarat to Leicester in the 1970s, describes Diwali as “the time when our whole family comes together. The children help make rangoli at the door; we do arati together; we share sweets with the neighbours. It keeps us Hindu even in England.” For the British Hindu community, Diwali is both a religious festival and a powerful expression of cultural identity and continuity.

The festival includes: lighting of diyas and candles in the home; performance of Lakshmi puja on the main night; exchange of gifts and sweets; fireworks; and in larger communities, public processions and light displays. The lighting of the home symbolises the divine light entering and blessing the household.

Each of the five days of Diwali has its own significance. Day 1 (Dhanteras) — prayers for prosperity and wealth, associated with Lakshmi and Kubera (the god of wealth). Day 2 (Choti Diwali / Naraka Chaturdashi) — associated with Krishna’s defeat of Narakasura in South Indian tradition; symbolic cleansing. Day 3 (Diwali / Lakshmi Puja) — the main night, with Lakshmi puja, diyas and fireworks; the most important day of the festival. Day 4 (Govardhan Puja / Padwa) — associated with Krishna lifting the Govardhan hill; celebrations of new year in some regions. Day 5 (Bhai Dooj) — celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.

Holi: Origins and Meaning

Holi is celebrated in late February or March, at the full moon that marks the end of winter and the arrival of spring. It is known as the Festival of Colours. The name Holi comes from Holika, a demoness who features in one of the festival’s origin stories.

The main origin story involves the demon king Hiranyakashipu, who demanded that everyone worship him instead of God. His own son, Prahlada, refused — he was a devoted worshipper of Vishnu. Hiranyakashipu tried many times to kill Prahlada, but Vishnu protected him each time. Finally, Holika (the demon king’s sister) tried to burn Prahlada in a fire, but Holika herself was burned while Prahlada emerged unharmed. This is the theological meaning of the bonfire (Holika Dahan) lit on the eve of Holi: the destruction of evil and the protection of the devoted.

A second strand of Holi’s meaning comes from the story of Krishna and Radha. Krishna, as a young man in Vrindavan, playfully sprayed coloured water on Radha and the gopis (cowherd women). This playfulness became the tradition of throwing coloured powder and water at Holi — a joyful, egalitarian celebration in which social distinctions are temporarily dissolved.

Key Fact

Holi has two main meanings: (1) the triumph of devotion over evil — Prahlada’s devotion to Vishnu protecting him from Holika; (2) the joyful, playful love of Krishna and Radha — the throwing of colours expresses the exuberance of bhakti devotion.

Holi in Great Britain Today

Holi has grown significantly in visibility in Britain. Hindu communities gather for Holika Dahan (the bonfire on the eve of Holi) and then the colour celebration the following day. University Hindu Societies across the UK hold Holi events that attract both Hindu and non-Hindu students. The Bhaktivedanta Manor in Hertfordshire holds a celebrated Holi festival.

Dev, a 19-year-old student at a UK university, describes Holi as “the one festival where being Hindu feels completely joyful and free. The colours, the music — it feels like the tradition is saying: God loves joy.” For many young British Hindus, Holi’s themes of renewal, joy and the equality of all people give it particular resonance in a multicultural society.

The theological significance of Holi includes: renewal and the transition from winter to spring; the triumph of dharma (right conduct and devotion) over adharma (evil); the equality of all people before God — during Holi, social hierarchies are temporarily set aside and all play together as equals.

Both Diwali and Holi celebrate the triumph of good over evil and are rooted in stories of Vishnu’s protective power (through his avatars Rama and Krishna, or directly in the case of Prahlada). Both are community celebrations with strong family dimensions. However, they differ in character: Diwali is primarily a devotional festival with puja, lamps and prayers for prosperity — it has a more formal religious character. Holi is primarily a festival of joy and social renewal, with its emphasis on colour, play and equality — its religious dimension (Holika Dahan) sits alongside a more exuberant, popular celebration. This contrast is worth noting in any exam question that asks you to compare two Hindu festivals.
exam_tip_html:
For a 6-mark Explain question on Hindu festivals, a typical stem is “Explain two reasons why Diwali is important for Hindus in Britain today.” You must name a source — the Ramayana is the primary textual source for Diwali (Rama’s return to Ayodhya). Name the Ramayana, state what it says (Rama returned after defeating Ravana and the people lit lamps), and develop two reasons (e.g. community worship and Lakshmi puja for prosperity; cultural identity for British Hindus). Without a named source, you are capped below Mastering.

Common error: students describe Holi only as “a festival where Hindus throw coloured powder.” The top-band response explains the theological meaning: the destruction of evil (Holika Dahan), the victory of Prahlada’s devotion to Vishnu, and the joyful bhakti associated with Krishna and Radha. Describe the practice and its meaning.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Diwali is the Festival of Lights, celebrated in autumn. Its primary Hindu meanings are: the return of Rama to Ayodhya (Ramayana) and the worship of Lakshmi for prosperity. Lamps, rangoli and puja mark the festival; in Leicester, it is a major public celebration.
  • Holi is the spring Festival of Colours. Its theological meanings are: the triumph of Prahlada’s devotion to Vishnu over the evil of Holika (Holika Dahan), and the joyful love of Krishna and Radha. The throwing of colours expresses equality and the exuberance of bhakti.
  • Both festivals reinforce core Hindu themes: the triumph of dharma over adharma, the power of bhakti devotion, and the importance of community and family. For British Hindus, they are also expressions of cultural identity and continuity.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the meaning of the Holika Dahan bonfire at Holi?
A) It represents the burning of old clothes to welcome spring
B) It symbolises the destruction of the demoness Holika and the triumph of devotion over evil
C) It is a secular celebration of the end of winter
D) It represents Rama's victory over the demon Ravana
practice_questions.marks: B) It symbolises the destruction of the demoness Holika and the triumph of devotion over evil [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the goddess whose worship is central to the main night of Diwali.
Give two ways in which Diwali is celebrated by Hindus in Britain today.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable answers: lighting of diyas and candles in the home to welcome Lakshmi; performance of Lakshmi puja on the main night; decoration of homes with rangoli; exchange of gifts and sweets; community gatherings and processions (e.g. Leicester's Belgrave Road celebrations); fireworks; visiting the mandir for special puja services.

practice_questions.text:
Parveen is a 15-year-old Hindu girl preparing for Holi with her family in Birmingham. She asks her grandmother why the festival involves throwing coloured powder.
Explain two reasons why the throwing of colours at Holi is meaningful for Hindus.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable reasons: the colours recall the playful story of Krishna and Radha at Vrindavan — the joyful expression of bhakti love; the throwing of colours on all people equally symbolises that before God all are equal — social distinctions are dissolved during Holi; the festival celebrates the arrival of spring and the renewal of the natural world, which Hindus understand as God's creation; the colour represents the exuberance and joy of devotion.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Diwali is an important festival for Hindus.
Refer to a sacred writing or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons with a named source integrated. Primary source: the Ramayana (Rama's return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana — the lighting of lamps celebrated his return and the triumph of righteousness). Reason 1: Diwali reaffirms core Hindu beliefs about dharma — Rama's story teaches that truth and righteousness will ultimately triumph over evil, giving worshippers confidence in the cosmic moral order. Reason 2: Lakshmi puja connects the festival to daily Hindu life — the prayers for prosperity and wellbeing at Diwali reflect the purushartha of artha (material wellbeing as a legitimate aim of life), and the lighting of the home symbolises inviting divine grace into everyday existence. Sub-tradition contrast (different Diwali stories in Vaishnavite/South Indian traditions) earns further credit. Secure: Two reasons, source referenced. Developing: One reason without development. Emerging: Basic description of practices.

practice_questions.text:
'Holi is a more important festival than Diwali for Hindus in Britain today.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Holi's themes of equality, joy and the renewal of community may be especially resonant for British Hindus living in a multicultural society where social divisions are a daily reality. Holi has grown significantly in public visibility in Britain — university events, Bhaktivedanta Manor's Holi celebration. Holi's joyful, accessible character may appeal to younger generations and bridge Hindu and non-Hindu communities in a way that Diwali's domestic puja does not. Arguments against: Diwali is far more widely recognised as a Hindu festival in British public life and has greater public impact (Leicester's celebrations, public lighting events, Diwali cards). The religious depth of Diwali — Lakshmi puja, the return of Rama — gives it a more explicitly devotional character. For most Hindu families in Britain, Diwali is the festival at which the whole family gathers and which most directly expresses devotion to God through puja. The Ramayana's story of Rama's return is one of the most beloved narratives in the Hindu tradition and gives Diwali deep theological grounding. Non-religious view: A humanist might value both festivals for their community-building functions and the joy they bring, without accepting their theological claims. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that both festivals serve important but different functions — Diwali is more central to formal devotional practice and cultural identity in Britain, while Holi is increasingly important for community integration and for younger Hindus. The statement is therefore an overstatement — both are important, serving different needs. Mastering: Full range, named sources, sub-tradition contrast, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Description only.

knowledge_checks.q: Which Hindu epic provides the primary origin story for Diwali?
Which story about Holi involves a young boy's devotion to Vishnu protecting him from evil?
options: The story of Rama and Ravana
The story of Krishna and Radha
The story of Prahlada and Holika
The story of Arjuna and Krishna

knowledge_checks.q: The word 'Diwali' comes from the Sanskrit for 'row of _____'.
The bonfire lit on the eve of Holi is called Holika _____.
Match each festival element to its meaning:
right: Welcoming Rama home and symbolising the triumph of light over darkness
Praying for prosperity and inviting divine blessing into the household
Celebrating the joyful love of Krishna and Radha; expressing equality before God

flashcard_questions.a: The Hindu festival of lights, celebrated in autumn, associated with Rama's return to Ayodhya and Lakshmi puja.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main origin story of Diwali?
flashcard_questions.a: Rama's return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana — the people lit lamps to welcome him home (Ramayana).

flashcard_questions.q: Which goddess is worshipped on the main night of Diwali and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Lakshmi — goddess of wealth and prosperity. Hindus perform puja to welcome her blessing into the home.
The bonfire lit on the eve of Holi, symbolising the destruction of the demoness Holika and the triumph of good over evil.

flashcard_questions.q: Who is Prahlada and why is he important at Holi?
flashcard_questions.a: A devoted worshipper of Vishnu whose faith protected him when his aunt Holika tried to burn him — his survival symbolises devotion triumphing over evil.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Krishna and Radha story associated with Holi?
flashcard_questions.a: Krishna playfully sprayed coloured water on Radha at Vrindavan — this became the tradition of throwing colours at Holi.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the throwing of colours at Holi represent?
flashcard_questions.a: The joyful love of Krishna and Radha; the equality of all before God; renewal and the arrival of spring.

flashcard_questions.q: Where are Diwali celebrations particularly significant in Britain?
flashcard_questions.a: Leicester's Belgrave Road — one of the largest Diwali celebrations outside Asia.
Intricate patterns made from coloured powder, created at the entrance to Hindu homes at Diwali to welcome Lakshmi.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Diwali differ in meaning between Hindus and Sikhs?
flashcard_questions.a: For Hindus, Diwali marks Rama's return and Lakshmi worship. For Sikhs, it is Bandi Chhor Divas — marking Guru Hargobind's release from imprisonment.

glossary_terms.definition: The Hindu festival of lights, celebrated in autumn, associated with Rama's return to Ayodhya and the worship of Lakshmi.
The Hindu spring festival of colours, celebrating the triumph of devotion over evil (Prahlada and Holika) and the love of Krishna and Radha.
The bonfire lit on the eve of Holi, symbolising the destruction of the demoness Holika and the triumph of good over evil.
One of the two great Hindu epics — the story of Rama, an avatar of Vishnu, his wife Sita and his victory over the demon king Ravana.
Intricate patterns made from coloured powder, used to decorate Hindu homes at Diwali to welcome Lakshmi.
A small clay oil lamp used in Hindu worship and at festivals, especially Diwali, symbolising the triumph of light over darkness.

hero_image_caption: Diwali lamps and Holi colours — two of the most joyful expressions of Hindu devotion in Britain today.
